temptingClaims: A moving sphere would look flattened, as a photograph of it would show.
whyTempting: § 4 says that a moving sphere, viewed from the stationary system, has the shape of an ellipsoid, and “viewed” sounds like seen.
whereItIsTrue: The shape § 4 finds is real in its own sense: it is where the surface is at one time of the stationary system, as measured with that system's rods and synchronized clocks.

whatIsTrue.r0: § 4's ellipsoid is the set of positions the surface occupies at one instant of the stationary system. A photograph records light that left different parts of the body at different times, which is a different question.
whatIsTrue.r1: § 4 takes a rigid sphere of radius \(R\) at rest in the moving system and writes the equation of its surface in the coordinates \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) of the stationary system at the time \(t = 0\): \(\frac{x^2}{\left(\sqrt{1-(v/V)^2}\right)^2} + y^2 + z^2 = R^2\). Measured in the state of motion, viewed from the stationary system, the body has the shape of an ellipsoid of revolution with axes \(R\sqrt{1-(v/V)^2}\), \(R\), \(R\) (p. 903). “At the time \(t = 0\)” is the point: the shape is built from positions taken simultaneously in the stationary system, by the clocks § 1 synchronizes. SR-03's sphere preset shows axes of 0.8 and 1 at 0.6 of the speed of light.
whatIsTrue.r2: (1) The sphere at rest in \(k\): every point of its surface lies at distance \(R\) from its centre. (2) Transform to \(K\) and fix one time, \(t = 0\): the equation becomes \(\frac{x^2}{1-(v/V)^2} + y^2 + z^2 = R^2\) (p. 903). (3) Read off the axes: along the motion \(R\sqrt{1-(v/V)^2}\), across it \(R\). At \(v = 0.6V\) that is \(0.8R\) and \(R\). (4) Each point of that surface is a position at the same time of \(K\), found with rods and synchronized clocks. (5) A camera collects light arriving at one moment, which left nearer and farther parts of the body at different times, so a photograph answers a different question from the one § 4 answers.
whatIsTrue.r3: What a moving body would look like in a photograph is a later problem, solved with the light-travel times this entry mentions. The paper does not treat it, and this entry does not describe its solution.

sources: A. Einstein, Ann. Phys. (4) 17, 891–921 (1905), plate p. 903
